stories.body:
On the Bering Sea, Unalaska is the US’s most productive seafood port, employing thousands of workers. But Trump’s cuts, and his disastrous war with Iran, have caused chaos – and put Republican control of Congress at risk

It was less than 17 hours until the start of Alaska’s lucrative Bering Sea crab season, and Oystein Lone was standing on a dock in the city of Unalaska, preparing to embark in rough conditions.

The problem wasn’t the next day’s forecast of 60mph gusts, which would kick up white-capped swells and make crabbing, already one of the most dangerous jobs in the United States, even more hazardous. Nor was it the question of whether there’d be enough red king, tanner and snow crabs to go around – state regulators had, in fact, announced higher quotas for the season.

What was bothering Lone, as the sun sank lower in the sky that Wednesday evening, was the question of how to make the numbers work when diesel cost more than ever , thanks to the war with Iran.

“This is the most challenging time I’ve seen,” said Lone, who has been fishing since 1989. He had already spent $86,000 to put 12,000 gallons of the fuel in one of his two boats, but the price had climbed higher since then, and if he wanted to fill up again, he expected to spend $100,000.

Located further west than the Hawaiian islands, Unalaska is closer to Beijing, Tokyo and Seoul than Washington DC. Most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage, which cost at least $1,600 round trip and are prone to cancellation, due to the region’s unpredictable storms and fog.

But Unalaska is by no means a backwater. It has been the country’s most productive seafood port by volume for more than two and a half decades, and when its crab and pollock seasons are open, thousands of deckhands and processors arrive from elsewhere to work tough but well-paying jobs on boats offshore and in seafood plants crowded in the city.

Even here, the impacts of Donald Trump’s efforts to remake the US government in his image can be felt. Since Trump returned to the White House, the library, museum, public radio station and local government have had funding they relied on disrupted or canceled altogether. Longshoremen have been tasked with loading empty containers on to ships to avoid tariffs. And the soaring price for diesel has squeezed not just the seafood industry, but all of the nearly 4,300 residents of the city, who rely on the fuel for electricity.

“This whole town runs on diesel,” said Daneen Looby, a longtime Unalaska resident who sits on the city council and owns the Norwegian Rat Saloon. With distributors upping the fuel surcharges she pays for food and alcohol shipments, Looby is thinking of raising her menu prices. “I didn’t want to, but I kind of have to, otherwise I’m going to become a charity.”

The midterm elections are on Tuesday, and Alaska is set to play a major role in determining if the president’s Democratic foes regain control of Congress . Alaska resoundingly backed Trump in the 2024 election, as did a majority of Unalaska voters, but Democrats believe the president’s plunging public approval ratings together with rising fuel prices have put its two-term Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, at risk of losing re-election to their nominee Mary Peltola, even as scandals rock her campaign.

Candidates only occasionally make the trip to Unalaska, and there are just a handful of campaign signs up around town, but outrage over the direction the country has taken since Trump returned to office is prevalent.

“I feel like we have a rogue government right now, and I don’t feel like the Republicans are doing their job,” Looby said. “I don’t understand why Congress isn’t getting more involved.”

‘In furtherance of the president’s agenda’

The name Unalaska derives from a word in the language of the Unangax̂ people who have lived on the island for thousands of years, and roughly translates to “near the mainland” for its proximity to Alaska’s southwestern peninsula.

Russian fur traders arrived in the middle of the 18th century, and eventually established a colony that came under American control when Washington purchased the Alaska territory in 1867. As the second world war approached, the US military built bases on the large, mountainous island of Unalaska and the smaller Amaknak island next to it, which were connected by a single bridge in the 1970s. In June 1942, Japan staged back-to-back air raids that killed dozens, and there are still concrete pillboxes and bunkers strewn all over town and on the tops of its treeless, windswept hills.

In 2023, the most recent year for which data is available, more than 780m pounds of catch valued at nearly $225m came through its port, Dutch Harbor, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration . Pollock, a versatile white fish, is the main product, and if you’ve eaten fish sticks, imitation crab or a Filet-O-Fish sandwich at a McDonald’s in Asia or the United States, its ingredients may well have been processed on Unalaska. The different species of crab found in the Bering Sea are also offloaded here, and the travails of that work are documented every year by camera crews who embark from Dutch Harbor to film the reality series Deadliest Catch .

As soon as he took office in 2025, Trump began signing executive orders billed as rooting out waste from the federal government, together with the efforts of Elon Musk’s now-shuttered “department of government efficiency”. Democrats and good governance groups said the campaign undermined important functions of government, and were of dubious legality .

One of Trump’s orders , signed in March 2025, attempted to dismantle a slew of federal agencies, including the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS). The little known office is the source of a yearly grant that Unalaska’s public library receives to buy books, and librarian Karen Kresh expected $6,000 last year, only to be told the money would not be coming.

“It had been stable and been reliable for years and years, and that was sort of a surprise to see that instability come up with that grant,” she said.

The main repository in the United States for cultural and natural history objects from the island chain is the Museum of the Aleutians in Unalaska. When Trump arrived in office, its staff was at work cataloging a large collection of artifacts dating back to the Russians’ first contact with the Unangax̂, funded by more than $347,000 in grant money from the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH).

At the beginning of April, the museum’s executive director, Virginia Hatfield, received a message saying the grant was being canceled because it “no longer effectuates the agency’s needs and priorities”, and that the funds would be reallocated “in a new direction in furtherance of the president’s agenda”. The cut put the project on hold, and Hatfield was forced to lay off six people.

“It’s very heartbreaking, and it kind of truncated important work,” she said.

Weeks later, Republicans in Congress approved legislation ending funding for public media outlets, which they have long accused of broadcasting news with a liberal bias. The decision had significant implications for Alaska, the largest state in the country which is full of small, remote communities – like Unalaska – unreachable by road, and where cellphone service can be unreliable.

That makes radio the best way to get word out when an emergency strikes, and the same day the Senate began debating whether to cut funding, the island’s public broadcaster KUCB was putting out warning of a potential tsunami. The wave did not arrive, and the station lost half of its budget after Trump signed the bill, said Lauren Adams, the general manager. In the months that followed, KUCB, along with other public media outlets nationwide, experienced a surge in giving from outraged listeners. It was also among more than a dozen Alaska stations to receive temporary funding from the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA).

The station now has reserves in the bank, Adams said, but no long-term solution to the question of how to stay open, with annual federal funding gone.

“When you get just this windfall fundraising from around the United States, what’s the sustainability of that?” Adams asked. “Eventually, we’re going to run out of those reserves and things that kept us going.”

Lost opportunities

The second Trump administration hasn’t solely been a disruptive force in Unalaska.

Iliuliuk Family & Health Services is the city’s only clinic, and deals with everything from checkups to emergencies. Soon, they will open a pharmacy that can replace the mail-order drugs most residents rely on, thanks to more than $400,000 from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program.

Created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’s main domestic policy legislation , the program was conceived to address concerns from Republicans that cuts to the Medicaid health insurance program for poor and disabled Americans included elsewhere in the legislation would put rural hospitals out of business.

Most of the Medicaid provisions have not taken effect yet , but hospitals nationwide remain concerned that even with the Rural Health Transformation money, they could lose patients vital to keeping their doors open. Christy Fassbender, Iliuliuk’s chief operating officer, said that is unlikely to be an issue in Unalaska.

“We have a very small Medicaid population. We are less than 6% for Medicare and Medicaid, and that is because this is a working town,” Fassbender said.

Nor has the chaos the federal government experienced when Trump first began his term been permanent. In June of this year, the Museum of the Aleutians was notified that the grant from the NEH was back on, though in the time that the funding was canceled, the project director and outreach specialist Hatfield hired found other work, and the professor who had excavated the artifacts providing a glimpse into Unalaska’s past died.

The IMLS eventually restored the funds the library uses to buy books. But recently, Kresh learned that the Federal Communications Commission was considering ending E-Rate, a program that helps the library and Unalaska’s school district provide internet access. If that were to happen, she said, the library would have to look for another way to cover the expense of offering the only free, public wifi in town, which residents and visitors rely on to apply for jobs and stay connected to the world. NEH grants that had been cut nationwide were restored after a lawsuit , and a different suit halted the closure of the IMLS.

Unalaska has felt other consequences of Trump’s presidency, for which there appears to be little recourse.

At Unisea, one of the largest seafood processors in the city, they’re rebuilding their workforce after shifting away from foreign guest workers, visas which have long been hard to get and eventually became too unreliable, director of Alaska operations Ron Kjorsvik said.

The only foreigners still doing the difficult work of processing pollock, crab, black cod and halibut are 15 Ukrainians on a special visa for nationals of the war-ravaged country, but they’ll be leaving soon – none had their visas renewed, Kjorsvik said.

A group of congressional Democrats led by Virginia’s James Walkinshaw had complained to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) in March about delays processing such applications, and in a reply seen by the Guardian, the agency’s director said USCIS had “many competing priorities and urgent requests for consideration daily”, and could not “prioritize” Ukrainians with U4U visas.

Seafood processing plants on the islands, meanwhile, have their own generators supplying electricity, while the rest of the city runs on a separate, generator-powered grid. Unalaska’s leaders have long contemplated alternatives, including the possibility of tapping geothermal power from a nearby volcano.

Under Joe Biden, the Department of Energy (DOE) established the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, and Unalaska’s utility director, Erik Hernandez, said the city was in the process of applying for funds to install five one-megawatt wind turbines and a battery system on a windy parcel of land, which could have replaced most of their diesel generators. But after Trump took office, the DOE stopped communicating about the grant, and in June 2025, the city was informed the money was no longer available.

The DOE did not respond to a request for comment. Earlier this year, the US Government Accountability Office found that the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations had lost 85% of its staff over the first six month’s of Trump’s second term, and placed a stop work order on all contracts.

The city was as reliant on diesel as ever when the Iran war began and crude oil prices rose in tandem, and the fluctuating rate that Unalaska charges power users to cover the cost of fuel has climbed almost two thirds, from $0.22 per kilowatt hour last year, to as much as $0.36 now, Hernandez said.

The fuel price increase has furthered the stress on a fishing industry that was already not having a great year. Pollock in 2026 have been small and scarce, and storms have been frequent. That has meant less work for Dutch Harbor’s longshoremen who move refrigerated shipping containers filled with seafood onto ships bound for Asia or the US west coast. Shawn Schomer, the International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s shop steward at Matson, one of the major shipping lines serving the port, said he’s recently been getting a new and unusual request from his superiors.

Certain shipping containers that remain for too long in the United States are considered imports, and thus subject to the tariffs Trump has slapped on trading partners globally.

“We got to get these tariff cans out of here. That’s what the management tells us,” when it asks for the containers to be loaded on outgoing vessels, Schomer said.

“It can’t be good business to bring in empties and then have to sort them and ship them back out empty,” he said. A spokesperson for Matson declined to comment.

‘We’re at the bottom’

Lone, 58, has spent his adult life fishing, and expects the high price of diesel to ripple through his industry. Crew members can make six figures in a season, and will see less money, since vessels’ overhead impacts their pay, and the price boats get for their catch could also fall, because processors and shippers will similarly be looking to offset their fuel costs.

“Unfortunately, we’re at the bottom. We take the beating,” Lone said. “Everybody else just passes on their cost to us.”

He wonders if some of the Republicans he had previously trusted to stand up for Alaska’s interests in Washington DC were doing their job.

“I support Sullivan and Begich, but I’m not too sure if they’re doing much for us,” he said, referring to the state’s junior senator and congressman, Nick Begish, respectively. While Lisa Murkowski, the senior senator, has opposed the Iran war and the effort to cut public media funding, Sullivan and Begich supported both, and are facing fierce challenges to their re-elections this year.

As he waited to unload a 135-ton haul of pollock, CJ Peterson, captain of the trawler the Pacific Challenger, said he had been contemplating how much more his business could take. One of Alaska’s native corporations owns his vessel, and Peterson knows the grim economics could some day keep him and his crew on land.

“If the fish price doesn’t match the fuel costs, they’ll shut us down,” Peterson said.

Captain Chris Studeman was not waiting for that to happen. The evening before the noontime start of crab season, he gassed up his boat, the Kevleen K, at one of Unalaska’s marine fuel terminals, and tried not to think about how much more he was paying this year than last.

“Don’t have much choice,” Studeman yelled from the bridge, as his crew prepared the vessel, painted white and green and laden with crab pots, to cast off. “Can’t really change your plan. You just got to go for it.”

And with that, he turned to port and headed north-east, away from Unalaska and into the Bering Sea.

Published 1 November 2026

The Green Party is at a "crossroads" and needs to focus on its "core values", a former party co-leader has told the BBC, weeks after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

Adrian Ramsay suggested the Greens need their policies to appeal to a majority of British voters if they want to bring the "environmental changes that we need" and advised against taking an approach that risks being "quite divisive".

Green Party leader Zack Polanski responded by saying there was "no environmental justice without social, racial and economic justice".

The motion, which Polanski did not take part in or vote upon, defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" that had led to the "disenfranchisement and destruction" of Palestinians.

I would not have voted for Zionism motion, Polanski says Published 9 October

It backed the creation of a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales adopted the policy motion last month.

It led to a backlash from some Jewish groups, as well as criticism from senior Green figures, including Ramsay and other Green MPs.

Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski , who is Jewish, from entering the country.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission also wrote to the Green Party asking for more information about the motion after concerns were raised by dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners.

Labour later said it would end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disowned the policy.

Speaking to Newscast , Ramsay replied "no, it's not" when asked if he thought Zionism is racist before adding he agreed with Polanski and others in believing that what is happening in Gaza is "appalling".

The MP for Waveney Valley, who joined the party in 1998, said he does think Israel has a right to exist, something Polanski has stopped short of saying.

The Fight For The Future Of The Green Party

Newscast

Available now

Ramsay also said he has made it clear he is "deeply uncomfortable" with the motion adopted and suggested there is an "opportunity to take some action in relation to the motion in the run-up" to the party's spring conference next year.

He said the question now is how Polanski and the party as a whole responds to the motion.

Ramsay said: "I think there's a real crossroads point for the party at the moment.

"One option is to sort of dig in more down this approach, not only in relation to this motion, but I think that there's a risk it brings with it - a quite divisive, a quite internally focused approach to politics."

Ramsay said this is "perhaps seen from small groups of people on the hard left of politics who go around different parties try to influence how those parties are run".

He added: "What I want to see is the party really focus back in on our core aims as a party and our core values."

Ramsay said this includes ensuring the party is "consensus-building in how we approach our politics" and that "we engage the grassroots of our membership".

He added the party needs to be "very externally focused, because we're only going to be able to bring the environmental changes that we need to have to safeguard our society for now and for the future if the majority of the British public come behind that".

Ramsay served as co-leader of the Greens from 2021 to 2025 alongside Carla Denyer, who is also now an MP.

He unsuccessfully stood on a joint ticket with fellow MP Ellie Chowns in 2025, with the pair losing to Polanski in the leadership contest .

Polanski, who missed the conference vote to unsuccessfully campaign for election in a Westminster by-election, previously said he wants to see the "imperfect" motion amended in future.

However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

Australia’s central bank expected to hit mortgage holders again on Tuesday, as war in Middle East combines with collapsing house prices

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, major bank economists say, as the Reserve Bank is forced to keep interest rates higher to rid the nation of persistent inflationary pressures.

The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, in a move that will push the cash rate to its highest since 2008 amid rising worries the economy could even be tipped into recession.

Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, said the extended Middle East conflict, collapsing house prices and a more aggressive central bank would drive real GDP down to just 1% by the middle of next year, nearly half the previous estimate of 1.8%.

Growth through 2027 would be barely stronger at an estimated 1.1%, according to the updated projections.

Allen said she had expected to see “signs of economic recovery” by the New Year, but now sees the economy “bottoming deeper and later”.

This more pessimistic outlook was “mainly given oil has been a lot higher than we had been expecting,” she said.

“Most people thought we would see a resolution to the Middle East conflict by now and oil [prices] looking more normal. Alas, that has not been the case.”

Instead, Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, has surged from about $US72 a barrel in early July, to back above $US110 in recent days as the conflict broadens and hopes for a peace deal in the near future have all but disappeared.

After Jim Chalmers last month warned the December mid-year budget update would show a more pessimistic economic outlook , analysts at NAB also revealed a major downgrade to their forecasts.

Gareth Spence, the bank’s head of Australian economics, said “unemployment might need to rise higher than we thought” in order to get inflation back under control – a view he said reflected recent comments by top RBA officials.

The economy would grow below trend over 2027 and 2028, Spence said, echoing the forecast of just 1% growth next year.

after newsletter promotion

Spence forecast the key jobless measure would need to rise from 4.7% to as high as 5.4% by the end of next year, as the RBA doubles down on its battle to regain control of inflation.

The CBA forecast was more optimistic, seeing unemployment peak at 5.1% over the same timeframe.

Either way, the RBA’s multi-year strategy of bringing inflation to heel without sacrificing post-Covid employment gains now looks unlikely to be achieved.

As union leaders protested against the anticipated rate hike in front of the RBA’s offices in Sydney on Monday morning, Spence said the risk was that the central bank would have to hike again.

The deteriorating economic outlook comes as new data showed Australia’s property slump remained on track to be one of the deepest on record.

Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said home prices could fall by as much as 15% before levelling off late next year, with Sydney property values already down by 10% from their recent peak.

Drawing from RBA research, Oliver said a property correction of that magnitude could deliver a substantial hit to the economy, as worried homeowners pull back on spending – a phenomenon known as the “wealth effect”.

A weakening property market will also weigh on homebuilding, Oliver said, adding to the multiplying pressures on the economy.

While an economic contraction was not his “base case”, he warned there was a “significant and rising” risk of recession, the chance of which would rise to as high as 45% should the RBA hike as expected on Tuesday.

“We don’t know the tipping point.”

Somerset MP Anna Sabine says she uses a microphone in Parliament to take part in debates

Published 1 November 2026

The "whispering MP" who feared she may never be able to speak confidently again revealed she has seen signs of recovery after suffering nerve damage to her vocal cords during surgery.

Liberal Democrat Anna Sabine lost her voice for several months following a thyroid operation in June, which cut one of the nerves to her vocal cords, leaving her with a condition called vocal cord paralysis.

The MP for Frome and East Somerset said the loss of her voice had made her want to "hide" when Parliament returned in September.

But in a surprise turn of events, Sabine said she awoke a few weeks ago to find it had regained some of its natural strength and "broadly speaking, it's back to where it should be".

Bid launched for 410 new homes near motorway Published 1 day ago

Dog wedding chauffeurs and doggy roasts: The rise of the puppy experience economy Published 1 day ago

Dying patient left in pain by care delays, MP says Published 2 days ago

The 46-year-old said she first realised something was wrong when she woke up from surgery in hospital in Bath.

"I had been warned it might feel strange, so I was trying to reassure myself hopefully this was just what it was going to feel like," she said.

"But the next morning, my surgeon did come around and say, 'I'm really sorry, but there has been a mistake and we have caused permanent damage'.

"At that time I could speak, but only just. I was kind of whispering."

When Parliament returned after the summer, she had to use a microphone to take part in debates.

'I can't hide away'

Sabine said the experience had been a shock and had left her feeling quite lonely.

"Your voice is a really key point of who you are, whether you are an MP or not," she said.

"When I came back to work in September I really wanted to hide, I did not want to speak in the chamber with my voice, because it actually, at that point, when you stood up to speak, you weren't really sure what was going to come out."

She added: "But over that summer, I had heard from so many people because I'd done various radio and TV about it, and people had emailed me.

"I can't now hide away, so I kind of felt inspired by them really to stand up in the chamber, which I did feel really embarrassed about. Even though no-one made me feel embarrassed, it felt extremely exposing."

Sabine said she would be doing a campaign about getting more therapy for adults.

Her voice is now the closest since the surgery to how it was before.

"During recess, one morning I woke up and my voice was like it is now, and my family said 'Your voice is stronger'," she added.

stories.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
stories.summary: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo was a hit with people willing to spend $2,000 on a new mobile.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 hour ago

The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.

John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.

While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack .

The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.

"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.

Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.

Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.

During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.

Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.

Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.

Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.

However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.

Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."

Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.

Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.

Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.

Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.

As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.

Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."

It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

stories.title: Reeves says UK's future should be inside the EU
stories.summary: In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Rachel Reeves says Brexit has made the UK "poorer, weaker and less secure".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 1 November 2026

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves has argued the UK's future should be inside the EU, and that Brexit has made the country "poorer, weaker and less secure".

In her first major intervention since leaving the Treasury, Reeves said she welcomed debate around the UK's relationship with Europe.

At the last election, Labour's manifesto said a Labour government would stay outside the EU and make Brexit work.

But Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there needs to be an honest discussion about what the future relationship looks like.

The Conservatives have said there is no desire to rerun the Brexit debate and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has said there is no mandate to pursue closer EU ties.

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Burnham has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is next due by 2029.

In the Sunday Times , external , Reeves wrote: "No-one in the Treasury ever doubted where my instincts were. I do believe Britain's future lies in the European Union."

She said supporters of rejoining the EU had to "make the argument, demonstrate tangible benefits and to get the next steps right".

Reeves added that at the forthcoming UK-EU summit, she hoped for confirmation of the youth mobility scheme she has been pushing for since she was in office.

She also said she was hoping for "progress towards entry" into the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) scheme.

Announced last March, SAFE is part of an EU-wide effort to rearm after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

A defence pact agreed with the EU last May paved the way for UK-based defence companies to be part of projects funded by SAFE.

In her piece for the Sunday Times, Reeves also sought to defend her record in office.

She wrote about the need for governments to be "braver" in building big infrastructure projects and "clear eyed" about the risks and benefits AI would drive in advanced economies.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said she "can't even believe we are reopening" the Brexit debate.

She told BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "This is not something that is needed in order to cut welfare, in order to spend money on defence.

"We are having yet another Westminster bubble argument about the EU when it is time for us to actually start using the opportunities, fix mistakes that have been made and go into the future."

Badenoch added: "I do not want to indulge Andy Burnham's fantasies about redoing the referendum because he doesn't have a plan for what to do today."

Burnham told Badenoch during the most recent session of Prime Minister's Questions that he was focused on "getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility".

The next UK-EU summit will take place in Brussels on 20 November.

"One step at a time," says Healey on ending the minimum wage gap between older and younger workers

Published 31 October 2026

The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.

In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.

Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

In a BBC interview broadcast on Sunday , Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?

"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.

It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.

Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.

"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.

"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."

"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

The chancellor also suggested that he is willing to make potentially big cuts to some areas of public spending, to get the country's debt falling.

The budget documents spell out real-terms reductions to some government departments in the years to come.

The likelihood of the government following through was questioned by the respected independent number cruncher, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) this week.

But asked if he would make big cuts, Healey said: "We've already demonstrated we are prepared to take hard decisions about the priorities in government."

Pressed on whether he would make cuts of more than 2% a year to some government departments, he added: "We will carry that through to the 10-year plan and the spending review next year."

"But in the budget I also set out the ways that we're preparing and the work we've got under way to prepare for those spending review decisions."

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said the "bulk" of spending cuts should be from the welfare budget, describing it as containing "astronomical sums".

She also proposed reducing the size of the civil service and reducing budgets in departments such as the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport.

On whether she would support cuts pencilled in by the government, Badenoch told the same programme: "What exactly are they cutting? I'm not against what they're doing but there's no detail."

Badenoch said she did not want to see cuts in frontline services but said there was a need to "bring down the cost of government".

Reflecting on the Budget, she said: "The chancellor had 98 different measures, a lot of them very piecemeal, none will make a difference.

"So living within our means, absolutely, we've got to do that. That will require cuts to government, but we are setting out the things very clearly that we're going to change, the bulk of which is in welfare. Other departments will have changes too."

stories.title: How do we make new economic ideas a reality? – Aditya Chakrabortty answered your questions
stories.summary: Guardian columnist, senior economics commentator and host of the new Radical Thinking podcast Aditya Chakrabortty answered your questions on the big ideas around economics, society and democracy, and his new podcast thegreatfatsby asks : Do you think the fact that Gabriel Zucman, who is a recognised authority on wealth tax is given more respect, time and attention by the mainstream media than Gary Stevenson, who has worked eloquently and tirelessly to spread the debate about the terrible consequences of inequality and whose ideas and analysis are almost identical is because of our cultural fixation on class prejudice? Aditya says: I’ve followed Gabriel Zucman (and Emmanuel Saez and Thomas Piketty ) for a long time, and find his work rigorous and thought provoking. I don’t always agree, but I appreciate their acceptance that taxes on wealth are part of the fight against ever-increasing inequality. I think Gary Stevenson is eloquent and compelling and is fighting a good fight. His book tells a story very well. But I don’t accept the insistence on a ‘wealth tax’ (as opposed to taxes on wealth) as being the only way we fight everything from inequality to the far right. We have to look at workers’ rights, housing, public ownership, greater democracy in economics and politics as well. In the age of algorithm, simple, strong messages cut through. But the truth is often more complex. Aditya says: What a nice question, Marija. I try to read a lot and write a diary. Unfortunately, I have the handwriting of a GP so I can’t read old entries.
